title: Editing My Iceland Photos from Start to Finish (Raw to Final)
creator: Freya Lindqvist Photo
description:
Full edit of three frames from my Iceland trip: a black sand beach, a glacier lagoon and a moody church.

This video is sponsored by Luminar Neo. Get 10% off with code FREYA10 at skylum.com/freya

Gear: Sony A7 IV, 16-35mm f/4, 70-200mm f/4
Presets: freyalindqvist.com/presets
Instagram: @freyashoots

sentences.t: Hey everyone, welcome back, today I'm finally editing the Iceland photos I've been sitting on since March.
I've picked three frames, the black sand beach, the glacier lagoon, and that little black church that everyone photographs.
Let's start with the beach, because honestly, straight out of camera, this one is a disaster.
The sky is completely blown out, and the sand is basically a grey smudge.
So I shot this at about midday, which is the worst possible light, but we were only there for an hour, so you work with what you get.
I'm doing this whole edit in Luminar Neo, so I'll drop the raw file in and start with the sky.
First thing, I'm going to use the Sky Enhancer slider, and you can see it brings back a little bit of texture in those clouds without touching the sand at all.
Now the sand, I'm going to mask it, and Luminar has this one-click masking thing that picks out the ground surprisingly well, look at that.
It even got the edge around the rocks, which normally takes me ages with a brush.
On that mask I'll pull the shadows up, add some structure, and drop the temperature just a touch so the sand actually reads as black and not muddy brown.
And then for the last bit, I'm going to use their Relight tool, which lets me add a bit of light in the foreground as if the sun was lower.
It's subtle, I'm only going to about fifteen, but it gives the whole thing depth.
Okay, before and after, and yeah, that's a completely different photo.
So, quick thing, this video is sponsored by Luminar Neo, and I genuinely use it for most of my landscape work now.
If you want to try it, it's a one-time purchase or a subscription, it works on Mac and Windows, and it plugs into Lightroom if that's still your main editor.
My link is in the description, and if you use code FREYA10 at checkout, you'll get ten percent off.
That's skylum dot com slash freya, code FREYA10.
Alright, the glacier lagoon.
This one I'm much happier with out of camera, because we came back at sunrise and the light was unreal.
The big thing here is the icebergs, they've got this incredible blue in them, and I don't want to oversaturate it into something cartoonish.
So I'm only bumping vibrance, not saturation, and I'm keeping an eye on the whites so the snow doesn't turn grey.
A lot of people overedit glacier shots, and I get it, it's tempting, but the real colour was already wild.
I'm going to crop this slightly tighter, though, because there's a tourist in a bright orange jacket in the left corner.
No offense to the tourist, great jacket, but it's pulling my eye.
Okay, so that one's done, it didn't need much, and I think that's a good lesson actually.
Sometimes the best edit is a crop and a tiny bit of contrast, and then you stop.
Now the church.
This was shot on a really overcast day, everything is flat and grey, and I actually love that for this one.
I want it to feel lonely, like you're the only person for miles, which, by the way, we absolutely were not.
There were three coach buses parked just out of frame.
So I'm going to desaturate the greens in the grass, push the blues in the shadows, and add just a little vignette.
And then a bit of grain, which I know is a controversial choice, but I think it suits the mood.
Yeah, look at that, that's the one I'm printing.
So that's the three, let me know in the comments which one's your favorite.
And if you want me to do a full video on how I plan shots for a trip like this, tell me that too.
See you in the next one.
